case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Arizona Supreme Court’s refusal to grant post-conviction relief—by holding that Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.1(g) barred Cruz’s claim despite the U.S. Supreme Court’s intervening decision in Lynch v. Arizona—rests on an “adequate and independent” state-law ground that prevents U.S. Supreme Court review.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.1(g) (post-conviction relief available when there has been a “significant change in the law”); and, in the background, the federal due process rule of Simmons v. South Carolina (parole-ineligibility information when future dangerousness is argued).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Cruz argues that Lynch v. Arizona (Lynch II) constituted a significant change in law under Arizona’s longstanding interpretation of Rule 32.1(g) because it repudiated Arizona’s prior, binding understanding of Simmons; therefore, Arizona’s denial of relief misapplied (or unpredictably narrowed) Rule 32.1(g) to avoid reaching the federal Simmons/Lynch merits, making the asserted state procedural ground not “adequate” to bar Supreme Court review and entitling him to relief/merits consideration.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Arizona contends that the Arizona Supreme Court applied Rule 32.1(g) as a state-law rule of finality and post-conviction procedure, concluding Lynch II did not create the kind of “significant change in the law” required for reopening Cruz’s case; because that decision rests on an independent state procedural ground (Rule 32.1(g)) that is adequate to support the judgment, federal review of the underlying Simmons/Lynch claim is barred.
key_precedents: State v. Lynch (Lynch I), 238 Ariz. 84, 357 P.3d 119 (2015)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that we ordinarily defer to a state court’s construction of its own collateral-review rules and that Johnson v. Lee and Walker v. Martin caution against treating discretionary or general finality rules as inadequate simply because they foreclose federal claims. But adequacy remains a federal question, and Lee v. Kemna and Ford v. Georgia make clear that even a generally valid rule cannot be applied in a novel, unforeseeable, or “exorbitant” manner that operates as a trap—particularly where it insulates an otherwise conceded Simmons/Lynch error. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito underscore, Lynch did not merely “apply” Simmons; it repudiated Arizona’s entrenched, binding contrary understanding, so Arizona’s categorical refusal to treat Lynch as “significant” looks less like neutral finality administration and more like an unexpected narrowing in this posture. A narrow, as-applied holding on adequacy (without rewriting Rule 32.1(g) or reaching the ultimate Simmons merits) best respects federalism while preserving the Court’s institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Lee v. Kemna and Ford v. Georgia frames this as an unforeseeable “exorbitant” application, but those cases involved state courts invoking procedural requirements in ways that departed from established practice to forfeit claims that litigants reasonably could not have anticipated. Here, Arizona applied a settled collateral-review finality standard—what counts as a “significant change in the law” under Rule 32.1(g)—and concluded that Lynch corrected Arizona’s prior misunderstanding of existing federal law rather than announcing a new rule, a quintessential state-law judgment about reopening final convictions. Johnson v. Lee and Walker v. Martin, which several colleagues cite, reinforce that even discretionary or flexible state procedural bars remain adequate absent a showing of novelty, discrimination, or manipulation; Cruz has not demonstrated the sort of irregular, case-specific trap condemned in NAACP v. Alabama or James v. Kentucky. Because adequacy remains a federal question but turns on whether the state ground is firmly established and regularly followed as applied, I would not treat Arizona’s characterization of Lynch as “not significant” as the kind of unforeseeable procedural innovation that permits us to disregard an otherwise independent state ground.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that we ordinarily defer to a state court’s construction of its own collateral-review rules and that finality interests are weighty, particularly in postconviction proceedings. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, adequacy is a federal question, and under Ford v. Georgia and Lee v. Kemna even a generally legitimate rule cannot be applied in a novel, unforeseeable, or “exorbitant” way that functions as a trap to defeat a properly presented federal claim. Here, Lynch II did not merely restate Simmons; it repudiated Arizona’s entrenched, binding contrary understanding, so Arizona’s categorical insistence that Lynch is not “significant” under Rule 32.1(g) looks less like regular administration (Walker v. Martin; Johnson v. Lee) and more like an irregular narrowing timed to foreclose review. Given the practical consequence—insulating a conceded Simmons/Lynch due process error in a capital sentencing context—I remain persuaded the asserted state ground is inadequate as applied.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s central point—deference to a state court’s construction of its collateral-review rule, and Johnson v. Lee’s recognition that even discretionary bars can be adequate—remains the strongest argument for Respondent, but it does not answer the federal adequacy question as applied. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Lynch did not merely “clarify” Simmons; it repudiated Arizona’s entrenched, binding contrary premise, making Arizona’s insistence that Lynch is not a “significant change” under Rule 32.1(g) look novel and outcome-driven in the Lee v. Kemna/Ford v. Georgia sense. Walker v. Martin helps only if the rule is firmly established and regularly followed in comparable circumstances, and here the record suggests an irregular constriction that operates as a trap to foreclose a plainly raised federal due process right at the most consequential stage—capital sentencing. On pragmatic, fairness-centered grounds, I cannot accept a procedural characterization that insulates an acknowledged Simmons/Lynch error from any merits forum.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that we ordinarily defer to a state court’s characterization of its own postconviction standards and that finality rules can be “adequate” even when they bar federal claims (Walker; Johnson). But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, adequacy remains a federal question, and under Ford and Lee v. Kemna we withhold adequacy when a generally valid rule is applied in an unforeseeable or “exorbitant” way that operates as a trap for a federal right. Here, Arizona’s insistence that Lynch II—an express repudiation of Arizona’s prior, binding Simmons understanding—is categorically not a “significant change” under Rule 32.1(g) looks like precisely the kind of novel constriction NAACP v. Alabama and James v. Kentucky caution against, rather than a firmly established, regularly followed application. Johnson and Walker would matter more if the State showed comparable, consistent treatment of decisions that overruled Arizona’s entrenched legal premises, but this record instead suggests an ad hoc move that insulates an acknowledged Simmons/Lynch error from any merits forum.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that we generally accept a state court’s construction of its own postconviction rules and that, under Walker v. Martin and Johnson v. Lee, discretionary or flexible bars can still be “adequate.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, adequacy remains a federal question, and Ford v. Georgia plus Lee v. Kemna forbid treating a state ground as adequate when it is applied in a novel, unforeseeable, or “exorbitant” way that operates as a trap for a plainly raised federal right. Here, Arizona’s refusal to treat Lynch’s repudiation of Arizona’s prior binding Simmons understanding as a “significant change” under Rule 32.1(g) looks less like neutral finality administration and more like an unexpected constriction aimed at insulating a conceded federal due process error from review. Respecting federalism does not require us to credit an unforeseeable procedural innovation that blocks any merits forum for the federal claim in a capital case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is the institutional one: we normally defer to a state court’s interpretation of its own collateral-review rules, and Johnson v. Lee/Walker v. Martin confirm that a firmly established, regularly followed procedural bar can be adequate even if it blocks a federal claim. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, adequacy is a federal question, and Lee v. Kemna/Ford v. Georgia prohibit an unforeseeable or “exorbitant” application that operates as a trap—especially where it uniquely insulates an otherwise conceded Simmons/Lynch error. Here, Arizona had treated its pre-Lynch view as binding law, and Lynch II expressly repudiated that entrenched understanding; characterizing that repudiation as categorically not “significant” under Rule 32.1(g) looks like the kind of novel narrowing that fails the “firmly established and regularly followed” requirement as applied. That narrow adequacy-as-applied disposition respects federalism and finality without allowing a one-off procedural recharacterization to defeat review in a capital case.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that we ordinarily accept a state court’s construction of its own collateral-review rules and that Walker v. Martin and Johnson v. Lee counsel deference when the rule is firmly established and regularly followed. But, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, adequacy is a federal question, and Ford v. Georgia and Lee v. Kemna require us to reject an application that is novel or unforeseeable in the circumstances; treating Lynch II’s express repudiation of Arizona’s binding Simmons framework as categorically not “significant” under Rule 32.1(g) reads like an ad hoc narrowing that functions as a trap for a plainly presented federal claim. Thomas’s characterization of Lynch as merely a “correction” of what federal law always required does not answer the adequacy problem, because the relevant notice and regularity inquiry turns on how Arizona had authoritatively administered Simmons before Lynch, and that record suggests the opposite of a settled, evenhanded practice. Given those limits on deference, I remain persuaded the asserted procedural bar is inadequate as applied, at least to the extent it blocks merits consideration consistent with Lynch.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that we owe substantial deference to Arizona’s construction of Rule 32.1(g), and that Johnson v. Lee/Walker v. Martin tolerate procedural flexibility—does not answer the federal adequacy question when the application is unforeseeable in context. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Arizona had an entrenched, binding misreading of Simmons that Lynch II squarely repudiated; treating that repudiation as categorically not “significant” looks like the kind of novel, outcome-linked constriction Ford v. Georgia and Lee v. Kemna deem inadequate. Beard v. Kindler’s allowance for discretionary rules still presupposes evenhanded, non-exorbitant use, and here the practical effect is to insulate an acknowledged Simmons/Lynch due process error in a capital case from any merits forum. Under my procedural-fairness, consequences-aware approach, that irregular application cannot fairly bar federal review.

John Roberts.reasoning: Arizona’s invocation of Rule 32.1(g) does not bar our review if, as applied here, it was not “firmly established and regularly followed” or amounted to an “exorbitant application of a generally sound rule.” Lee v. Kemna, 534 U.S. 362, 376 (2002); Beard v. Kindler, 558 U.S. 53, 60 (2009). Lynch v. Arizona made clear that Arizona’s prior understanding of Simmons was incorrect, and treating Lynch as not a “significant change in the law” under Rule 32.1(g) appears to be an unforeseeable narrowing that functions to insulate a federal due process claim from merits review. Because adequacy is a question of federal law and we must ensure state procedural rules are applied in a consistent, non-discriminatory way when federal rights are at stake, Walker v. Martin, 562 U.S. 307, 321 (2011), the asserted state ground is inadequate and we may reach the federal question (at least to require state merits consideration consistent with Simmons/Lynch).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: This Court lacks jurisdiction where the state judgment rests on an adequate and independent state ground, and Arizona’s application of Rule 32.1(g) is a state-law rule of finality governing when collateral review may be reopened for a “significant change in the law.” Nothing in the text of Rule 32.1(g) compels Arizona to treat Lynch as such a change, and this Court generally defers to a state court’s construction of its own postconviction procedures so long as the rule is firmly established and not a mere device to evade federal review. Under Johnson v. Lee, a consistently applied state procedural bar can be “adequate” even when it prevents consideration of a federal claim, and Cruz has not shown the kind of unforeseeable, novel procedural trap condemned in James v. Kentucky or NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson. Because the Arizona Supreme Court’s decision rests on its independent interpretation of Rule 32.1(g), federal review of the Simmons/Lynch merits is barred.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Rule 32.1(g) allows post-conviction relief upon a “significant change in the law,” and Arizona’s prior, binding view in Lynch I treated Simmons as effectively inapplicable in Arizona; Lynch II squarely repudiated that understanding. By labeling Lynch II as not “significant” notwithstanding that it overturned the State’s entrenched interpretation of controlling federal law, the Arizona Supreme Court applied Rule 32.1(g) in an unforeseeably cramped, outcome-driven manner that is not an adequate state ground. This Court has long held that novel or irregular state procedural constructions cannot defeat federal review when federal rights are plainly asserted, see NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, and Lee v. Kemna similarly rejects unexpected procedural traps as “adequate.” Accordingly, the state procedural bar does not preclude this Court’s review of the underlying Simmons/Lynch due process claim.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Arizona’s invocation of Rule 32.1(g) is not an “adequate” state ground where its application to Cruz’s Simmons/Lynch claim was unforeseeable and functionally operated to insulate a federal due process right from review. Under Lee v. Kemna and Beard v. Kindler, adequacy turns on whether the procedural rule is firmly established and regularly followed, not applied with “exorbitant formalism” to defeat a plainly raised federal claim. Lynch v. Arizona directly repudiated Arizona’s prior, binding misreading of Simmons, making it a paradigmatic “significant change in the law” under Rule 32.1(g); treating it otherwise is an unexpected narrowing that risks discrimination against federal rights, contrary to Walker v. Martin. Given the practical stakes in a capital case and the jury-information right recognized in Simmons and reaffirmed in Lynch, we should reach the merits rather than allow a novel procedural construction to bar review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.1(g) allows reopening when there has been a “significant change in the law,” and Lynch v. Arizona (Lynch II) squarely repudiated Arizona’s prior, binding understanding of Simmons by reaffirming that parole-ineligibility information is required when the State argues future dangerousness. Treating Lynch II as not “significant” is an unforeseeable narrowing of the state rule as Arizona had applied it, making the procedural ground not “adequate” to bar this Court’s review under the principle that novel state-law constructions cannot be used to defeat federal rights. See Ford v. Georgia and NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, and compare Walker v. Martin (adequacy holds absent a purpose or pattern to evade federal guarantees). Because the asserted Rule 32.1(g) bar is applied here in a way that effectively insulates a federal Simmons/Lynch claim, it should not preclude merits review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rule 32.1(g) allows reopening when there has been a “significant change in the law,” and the Arizona Supreme Court’s determination that Lynch v. Arizona did not qualify rests on a novel and unforeseeable constriction of its own rule given that Lynch squarely repudiated Arizona’s prior, binding understanding of Simmons. Under this Court’s adequate-state-ground doctrine, a state procedural bar is not “adequate” when it is applied in an unexpected or inconsistently applied way that functions to defeat a plainly raised federal right. See Ford v. Georgia and Lee v. Kemna; and because adequacy is itself a question of federal law, Beard v. Kindler confirms our authority to look past such an application. Accordingly, the asserted Rule 32.1(g) ground is inadequate to foreclose our review of Cruz’s Simmons/Lynch claim.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Arizona’s reliance on Rule 32.1(g) is not an adequate state ground because the Arizona Supreme Court applied the “significant change in the law” requirement in an unexpected, outcome-driven way after Lynch v. Arizona made clear that Arizona’s prior understanding of Simmons was wrong. Under this Court’s adequacy cases, a state procedural bar cannot defeat federal review when it is novel, unforeseeable, or inconsistently applied to block a plainly raised federal right. See Lee v. Kemna, 534 U.S. 362 (2002); James v. Kentucky, 466 U.S. 341 (1984); NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, 357 U.S. 449 (1958). Because Lynch II repudiated the state court’s prior “binding” interpretation, treating it as not significant under Rule 32.1(g) is not a workable, consistently applied rule of finality and therefore does not bar this Court’s review of the Simmons/Lynch claim.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Arizona Supreme Court’s invocation of Rule 32.1(g) to bar Cruz’s claim is not an “adequate” state ground because it applied the rule in a novel and unforeseeable way to avoid reaching the federal Simmons/Lynch issue. Lynch v. Arizona (Lynch II) expressly rejected Arizona’s prior, binding understanding of Simmons, and under Arizona’s own Rule 32.1(g) framework a decision that repudiates controlling law is the paradigmatic “significant change in the law.” Under NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson and Lee v. Kemna, a state procedural ruling cannot preclude federal review when it operates as a “springe” through an unexpected, irregular application of local practice. Because the asserted procedural bar was not firmly established and regularly followed as applied here, it cannot defeat this Court’s review of the federal claim.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Arizona’s reliance on Rule 32.1(g) is not an “adequate” state ground where its application is novel or unforeseeable in light of the State’s prior, binding misinterpretation of Simmons that Lynch v. Arizona (2016) squarely repudiated; a state procedural bar cannot be used in an unexpected way to evade review of a federal right. Under NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson and Lee v. Kemna, this Court will not treat a state-law ground as adequate when it is applied in a manner lacking fair notice or consistent administration, particularly where it effectively insulates an acknowledged federal error. Given Arizona’s entrenched pre-Lynch rule (as reflected in State v. Lynch (2015)) and Lynch II’s direct correction of that federal-law mistake, treating Lynch II as categorically not a “significant change in the law” under Rule 32.1(g) functions as an unfair, outcome-driven narrowing that should not bar merits review. Procedural fairness and the practical consequences in a capital case counsel against allowing finality doctrine to override meaningful enforcement of Simmons’ due process guarantee.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Arizona Supreme Court’s refusal to grant post-conviction relief under Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.1(g) (after the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Lynch II) rests on an “adequate and independent” state procedural ground that bars federal review, or instead improperly avoids enforcing petitioner’s federal due-process right under Simmons to inform a capital-sentencing jury of parole ineligibility.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.1(g) (post-conviction relief for a “significant change in the law”), as applied in a capital case implicating the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause through Simmons v. South Carolina’s rule requiring a parole-ineligibility instruction when future dangerousness is at issue and life without parole is the alternative to death.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Cruz argues that Lynch II constituted a significant change in law correcting Arizona’s previously incorrect, binding interpretation of Simmons (and related cases) and therefore fits within Rule 32.1(g). By denying relief without addressing the federal constitutional merits and by characterizing Lynch II as not a qualifying change, the Arizona Supreme Court applied Rule 32.1(g) in an unforeseeable or inconsistent way that is not an adequate and independent state ground; the result is that Cruz was denied the federal due-process protection recognized in Simmons and reaffirmed in Lynch II—namely, the right to have the jury told he was parole-ineligible when the State argued future dangerousness.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Arizona argues that the Arizona Supreme Court’s ruling is based on an adequate and independent state-law ground: Rule 32.1(g) did not permit relief because Lynch II did not amount to a qualifying “significant change in the law” under Arizona’s post-conviction framework (or, at minimum, the state court’s interpretation of its own rule controls). Because the decision rests on state procedural law rather than federal law, federal courts (including the U.S. Supreme Court) should not disturb the judgment; Cruz’s complaint that the state court did not discuss federal law underscores that the ruling was state-law-based.
key_precedents: State v. Lynch (Lynch I), 238 Ariz. 84, 357 P.3d 119 (2015)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to stress Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin: discretionary or context-sensitive state postconviction rules can be “adequate,” and we should not lightly second-guess a state court’s construction of its own collateral-review trigger. But as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan emphasize, adequacy remains a federal question, and Lee v. Kemna/Ford v. Georgia forbid treating a generally valid rule as adequate when applied in an unforeseeable, case-dispositive way that functions as a “springe” against a federal right. Arizona’s move to label Lynch II—which repudiated Arizona’s previously controlling view of Simmons—as “no significant change” effectively insulates a conceded Simmons error from any merits forum, and that irregular operation is precisely what our adequacy doctrine polices. A narrow holding confined to Rule 32.1(g) as applied in these circumstances respects finality while preventing States from recharacterizing this Court’s correction of a binding misinterpretation into a procedural bar.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that, under Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin, discretionary or context-sensitive state collateral rules may still qualify as “adequate,” and that Arizona may treat Lynch II as mere application of existing Simmons law to protect finality. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, adequacy is a federal question, and Lee v. Kemna/Ford v. Georgia forbid a State from applying a procedural rule in an unforeseeable, irregular way that functions as a “springe” to defeat a federal right; Arizona’s reclassification of Lynch II as “no significant change” after its prior, controlling view that Simmons did not apply has that character. Even giving full respect to state-law interpretation, the Supremacy Clause and our long-settled adequate-and-independent-ground doctrine do not allow a novel label for Rule 32.1(g) to insulate an acknowledged federal due-process error from any merits forum. Nothing in Justice Alito’s finality rationale shows that this particular application was firmly established and regularly followed rather than outcome-driven, so I adhere to Petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “springe” framing (invoking Lee v. Kemna and Ford v. Georgia) is the strongest point for Petitioner, but I do not think it fits this record: Arizona did not enforce a hypertechnical filing rule ad hoc to evade review; it gave a reasoned construction of the substantive trigger in Rule 32.1(g) (what counts as a “significant change in the law”) in light of its finality framework. Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin, which several colleagues acknowledge, confirm that even context-sensitive postconviction rules can be “adequate” absent a showing of irregular, targeted manipulation, and I do not see the kind of pattern condemned in NAACP v. Alabama or Davis v. Wechsler. That Lynch II corrected Arizona’s prior Simmons misunderstanding does not compel calling it “new law” for purposes of reopening final judgments; States may rationally treat a decision as an application/clarification of existing federal law without thereby creating a federally cognizable “springe.” Expanding adequacy to second-guess this state-law line-drawing—especially in capital collateral review—undervalues the State’s legitimate interests in orderly postconviction administration and finality.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin caution against treating discretionary or context-sensitive state postconviction rules as categorically inadequate, and that finality interests are weighty. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, adequacy remains a federal question, and Arizona’s application here looks like the kind of unforeseeable, merits-foreclosing “springe” condemned in Lee v. Kemna and James v. Kentucky: it reclassifies Lynch II—this Court’s repudiation of Arizona’s binding misreading of Simmons—as “no significant change,” thereby insulating a conceded due-process error from any merits review in a capital case. Even accepting Alito’s premise that Lynch II ‘applied existing law,’ the relevant practical reality is that Arizona law before Lynch treated Simmons as inapplicable; when this Court corrects that entrenched understanding, Rule 32.1(g) cannot be administered in a way that predictably bars the very claim the correction makes viable. On my pragmatic, fairness-focused view—especially where the consequence is an execution after a jury was denied constitutionally required parole-ineligibility information—the state ground as applied is not “firmly established and regularly followed,” so it cannot defeat federal review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that, under Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin, discretionary state postconviction rules can be “adequate,” and States have weighty finality interests; I agree we should not generally second-guess state collateral-review line-drawing. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, adequacy is still a federal question, and Arizona’s application of Rule 32.1(g) here operates like an unforeseeable reclassification: after Lynch II repudiated Arizona’s previously controlling misreading of Simmons, the state court called it “no change” in order to foreclose any merits forum for a conceded federal error. Lee v. Kemna and Ford v. Georgia matter because they show that even a generally valid procedural rule becomes inadequate when applied in an irregular, springe-like way that defeats a federal right, and that is the practical effect of Arizona’s move here. On a pragmatic textualist view, “significant change in the law” cannot coherently exclude a decision that displaced binding contrary state precedent and compelled different capital-sentencing instructions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin caution against treating discretion or line-drawing in state collateral rules as automatically inadequate, and we should respect state interests in finality. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, adequacy remains a federal question, and the touchstone is whether the asserted bar is “firmly established and regularly followed” rather than deployed in an unforeseeable, case-dispositive way (Lee v. Kemna; Ford v. Georgia). Arizona’s move to label Lynch II—this Court’s repudiation of Arizona’s controlling Simmons misreading—as “no significant change” functions in operation like a springe: it converts a correction of an entrenched state practice into a procedural reason never to reach a conceded federal error. Under a textualist/originalist understanding of our adequate-and-independent-state-ground doctrine and the Supremacy Clause’s demands, I cannot credit an irregular recharacterization that predictably insulates federal law from review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point—that Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin allow even discretionary postconviction rules to qualify as “adequate,” and that finality interests are substantial—does not, in my view, answer the key adequacy question here: whether the rule was firmly established and regularly followed as applied. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Arizona’s move to label Lynch II (this Court’s correction of Arizona’s entrenched Simmons misreading) as “no significant change” operates like the Lee v. Kemna/James v. Kentucky ‘springe,’ because it retroactively reclassifies a decision that displaced controlling state practice into “nothing new” and thereby blocks any merits review of a conceded federal error. Walker and Kindler counsel deference to neutral, evenhanded state administration, but they do not authorize an unforeseeable application that functionally insulates a federal constitutional claim from any forum. Given the institutional need for predictable, non-arbitrary procedural bars—especially in capital cases—I continue to think Rule 32.1(g) is inadequate as applied to bar federal review.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to stress, under Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin, that a discretionary state postconviction rule may still qualify as an “adequate” state ground and that finality interests permit meaningful limits on reopening. But adequacy remains a federal question, and as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, the dispositive issue is whether the rule is “firmly established and regularly followed” as applied, not whether it can be described as a plausible state-law construction in the abstract. Here Arizona’s treatment of Lynch II—this Court’s repudiation of Arizona’s binding misreading of Simmons—as “not a significant change” functions like the sort of surprise, case-ending “springe” Lee v. Kemna and Ford v. Georgia forbid, because it retroactively recharacterizes a controlling legal landscape to foreclose any merits review of an acknowledged federal constitutional error. That makes Rule 32.1(g), as applied in these circumstances, inadequate to bar federal review, so I remain with the Petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—grounded in Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin—is that discretionary, context-sensitive state postconviction rules can still be adequate, and that finality gives States room to refuse reopening when a decision merely “applies” existing federal law. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, adequacy remains a federal question, and Lee v. Kemna/Ford v. Georgia require us to look at real-world predictability and regularity, not labels: Arizona treated Simmons as inapplicable under its own binding precedent until Lynch II, then reclassified Lynch II as “no change” to block any merits forum for an acknowledged due-process violation. That sequence makes Rule 32.1(g) operate as a surprise, right-insulating springe rather than a firmly established and regularly followed bar as applied here—especially in a capital sentencing context where the practical consequence is execution after a jury was denied constitutionally required parole-ineligibility information. Beard and Walker therefore do not undermine my view; they permit discretion, but not the kind of unforeseeable recharacterization that defeats federal review.

John Roberts.reasoning: Arizona’s invocation of Rule 32.1(g) to deny relief after Lynch II appears to operate as an inadequate state procedural ground because it treats this Court’s correction of Arizona’s prior, binding misunderstanding of Simmons as not a “significant change in the law,” a characterization that is difficult to reconcile with the State’s own prior position and risks an unforeseeable or inconsistently applied bar. Under the adequate-and-independent-state-ground doctrine, a state procedural ruling cannot defeat review of a plainly presented federal claim when it functions as a novel or irregular “springe” to avoid enforcing federal rights. NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson and related cases teach that such procedural maneuvers do not insulate a judgment from federal review, particularly where the result is to deny a capital defendant the due-process protection recognized in Simmons and reaffirmed in Lynch II. A narrow disposition would therefore treat Rule 32.1(g), as applied here, as inadequate and remand for consideration of the Simmons claim on the merits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Arizona Supreme Court’s reliance on Rule 32.1(g) is not an adequate state ground where the rule is applied in a novel or unforeseeable manner to defeat a plainly raised federal right. Lynch II did not announce a new federal rule so much as correct Arizona’s prior refusal to apply Simmons, and treating that correction as not a “significant change in the law” appears designed to evade enforcement of the Fourteenth Amendment due-process requirement recognized in Simmons v. South Carolina. Under this Court’s adequate-and-independent-ground cases, a state procedural ruling cannot bar federal review when it is not “strictly or regularly followed” or is applied with “pointless severity” in the particular case. Because the state court’s application of Rule 32.1(g) functions to insulate an acknowledged Simmons error from any merits review, federal review is not barred.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Arizona Supreme Court expressly relied on Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.1(g) in concluding that Lynch II was not a “significant change in the law,” and a state court’s interpretation of its own post-conviction rule ordinarily supplies an independent state-law basis that bars federal review. Under Beard v. Kindler and Walker v. Martin, a discretionary or context-sensitive state procedural rule can still be “adequate” absent a showing that it is novel, unforeseeable, or applied in a pattern designed to evade federal rights; Cruz has not demonstrated the sort of “purpose or pattern” or “springes” condemned in NAACP v. Alabama and Davis v. Wechsler. Lynch II primarily corrected Arizona’s prior misapplication of Simmons, but that does not compel Arizona to reopen final judgments through its collateral-review framework where the State reasonably characterizes the decision as an application of existing federal law rather than a new rule. Given the substantial state interests in finality and orderly post-conviction administration—especially in capital cases—the procedural ground should be treated as adequate and independent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Arizona’s reliance on Rule 32.1(g) to deny relief is not an adequate state ground where the state court applied the rule in an unforeseeable or inconsistently narrow manner to avoid reaching a plainly presented federal due-process claim. Adequacy is a federal question, and a procedural bar must be “firmly established and regularly followed,” which this Court polices especially when state practice risks insulating constitutional error in a capital case. See Lee v. Kemna, 534 U.S. 362, 375–376 (2002); James v. Kentucky, 466 U.S. 341, 348–349 (1984); Beard v. Kindler, 558 U.S. 53, 60 (2009). Given Lynch II’s reaffirmation that Simmons v. South Carolina, 512 U.S. 154 (1994), requires a parole-ineligibility instruction when future dangerousness is argued and life without parole is the alternative, Arizona cannot deploy a novel procedural characterization of Rule 32.1(g) to defeat enforcement of that federal right.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 32.1(g) allows post-conviction relief for a “significant change in the law,” and Lynch II squarely repudiated Arizona’s prior, binding misreading of Simmons by holding that when future dangerousness is argued and the alternative sentence is life without parole, due process requires a parole-ineligibility instruction. By treating Lynch II as not a qualifying “change” simply because it applied “clearly established” federal law, the Arizona Supreme Court applied Rule 32.1(g) in an unpredictable, form-over-substance way that effectively insulates a conceded Simmons violation—an application that is not “firmly established and regularly followed” and thus is not an adequate state ground under Beard v. Kindler and Lee v. Kemna. Because the state procedural ruling operates to evade enforcement of a federal due-process right, the adequate-and-independent-state-ground doctrine does not bar federal review, and Cruz is entitled to merits consideration of his Simmons/Lynch claim.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Although States may apply their own post-conviction rules, federal courts must ensure the asserted state procedural bar is “adequate,” i.e., “firmly established and regularly followed,” and not novel or unforeseeable as applied. See Beard v. Kindler, 558 U.S. 53, 60 (2009); Ford v. Georgia, 498 U.S. 411, 423 (1991). Here, Arizona’s narrowing construction of Rule 32.1(g) to treat Lynch II as not a “significant change in the law,” despite Lynch II’s correction of Arizona’s prior misreading of Simmons, appears to function as an unpredictable recharacterization that frustrates enforcement of the federal due-process right Simmons guarantees when future dangerousness is argued and parole ineligibility is the alternative. Because that application is not an adequate state ground, federal review is not barred and the Simmons/Lynch II requirement must be given effect.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Federal review is not barred because the asserted state procedural ground is not “adequate” where it is not firmly established and regularly followed as applied, particularly when it functions to defeat a federal constitutional claim. Under Beard v. Kindler and Lee v. Kemna (drawing on James v. Kentucky), adequacy is a federal question, and a state court may not apply a procedural rule in an unforeseeable or irregular way to avoid adjudicating a federal right. Here, after Lynch II reaffirmed Simmons’s due-process requirement that a capital-sentencing jury be informed of parole ineligibility when future dangerousness is argued and LWOP is the alternative, Arizona’s refusal to treat Lynch II as a “significant change in the law” under Rule 32.1(g) appears to be the kind of unpredictable application that cannot foreclose federal review. Given the centrality and workability of the Simmons instruction rule and the need for evenhanded post-conviction procedures, I would vote to allow consideration of the federal due-process claim.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Although a state court’s interpretation of its own post-conviction rule ordinarily supplies an independent ground, it is not “adequate” to bar federal review when it is applied in a novel, unforeseeable, or inconsistently enforced manner to defeat a federal right. Here, Arizona’s refusal to treat Lynch II—this Court’s reiteration that Simmons applies notwithstanding Arizona’s contrary view in Lynch I—as a “significant change in the law” under Rule 32.1(g) functions to insulate an acknowledged misapplication of Simmons from correction, and thus resembles the sort of procedural “springe” rejected in Davis v. Wechsler and NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson. Given that Lynch II reaffirmed the federal due-process requirement to inform a capital jury of parole ineligibility when future dangerousness is argued, the state court’s constricted use of Rule 32.1(g) is not a strictly and regularly followed ground adequate to preclude review. Accordingly, the state procedural ruling should not prevent enforcement of the Simmons due-process right.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Federal review is not barred if the asserted state procedural ground is not “firmly established and regularly followed,” and adequacy is itself a question of federal law. Ford v. Georgia, 498 U.S. 411, 424 (1991); Beard v. Kindler, 558 U.S. 53, 60 (2009). Arizona’s application of Rule 32.1(g) to treat Lynch II—this Court’s correction of Arizona’s misreading of Simmons—as not a “significant change in the law” appears unforeseeable and inconsistent with a rule meant to capture postconviction relief when controlling law shifts, making the state ground inadequate under Ford/Lee v. Kemna, 534 U.S. 362, 375-76 (2002). Given the practical consequence in a capital case of denying a Simmons parole-ineligibility instruction where future dangerousness is argued, procedural fairness requires federal review rather than permitting a novel state-law characterization to insulate a federal due-process violation.
